clue.text: Aristotle unsure about game best unplayed

indicators.note: 'about' can mean around and round, so the letters are turned round into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the philosopher's name, taken letter for letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: The great philosopher is doubtful about some game that is better left unplayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unsure' reads as Aristotle's state of mind, but its letters join the philosopher's name as the fodder, all fifteen of them.
explanation.definitionFit: In this deadly gamble a player spins a revolver's cylinder with one live round and fires at their own head, so nobody should ever play it.

clue.text: Turns sanctimonious bugger in backward glance

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one group is placed within another
something looking backward faces the other way, so these letters are read from right to left

parts.note: to glance is to see briefly
PI is short for pious, here meaning self-righteous
sod is a British insult for an annoying person

explanation.surface: A self-righteous scoundrel twists round to sneak a look behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: Sod is mild British slang for an unpleasant person. 'Turns' looks like a verb, but it is a noun: a person may 'have one of their turns'.
explanation.definitionFit: A turn in the sense of a sudden attack of illness or nerves is also called an episode, as in a medical episode.

clue.text: One slips during trial of lag

indicators.note: something happening during a period falls within it, so one letter goes back inside the rest
what slips loses its footing and drops out of its place, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone loses their footing in the middle of a test of slowness.
explanation.walkthrough: The I in TRIAL slips out of its place and lands one step further along, between the A and the L.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail is to fall behind or move more slowly than others, just as to lag means to drop back.

clue.text: Illegally issued amidst a revolution involving untold number

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so the mixed letters take in an extra one
a revolution turns things over completely, so the letters are overturned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknown numbers

explanation.surface: Something put out unlawfully in the middle of an uprising that cost countless lives.
explanation.walkthrough: Samizdat is Russian for 'self-published': banned writing copied by hand and passed around in the Soviet Union.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names clandestine Soviet-era literature, privately reproduced and circulated without official approval, so it was by nature unlawfully put out.

clue.text: Making lax use of it

indicators.note: making something means building it from raw material, so these letters are formed into a new word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is being careless with something they have been given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is a coy old word for sex, so 'of it' means relating to sex; read whole, the clue is also a sly description of being sexually lax.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun 'it' is a familiar euphemism for intercourse, and an adjective meaning relating to that is sexual.

clue.text: Those with degrees dine out, inspired by good wishes

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one group is taken inside another

parts.note: GRATS is informal shorthand for congratulations

indicators.note: 'out' can mean in disarray, so these letters are knocked out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Graduates go out for a celebratory meal, buoyed by congratulations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those with degrees' suggests graduates, but the degrees are of angle: slopes are measured in degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: A slope's steepness is expressed in degrees of angle, so slopes are things that have degrees.

clue.text: Become apparent in last of coffee blend

indicators.note: the last of anything is its final part, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
to blend things is to merge them

explanation.surface: A flavour shows itself in the dregs of a coffee blend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blend' reads as a noun for a mix of beans, but it works as a verb meaning to combine.
explanation.definitionFit: To emerge is to come out into view, so something that emerges becomes visible or known.

clue.text: Signal most recent conversation — pronouncement while playing 1?

parts.note: signal as an adjective means notable or outstanding
the last one is the latest
to have words is to talk

explanation.surface: Someone sends a sign about the latest chat they have had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signal' looks like a verb or noun but is the adjective meaning remarkable. The 1 refers to 1 Down, RUSSIAN ROULETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase mocks an overconfident remark that is promptly disproved, such as 'It's not loaded' said just before pulling the trigger in that deadly game.

clue.text: Increase each client's capital

parts.note: to up something is to increase it
per means for each, as in ten pounds per person
a lawyer's or social worker's client is one of their cases

explanation.surface: A financial adviser promises to grow every customer's money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' suggests money in the surface, but it means a capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital letters are the larger letter forms, which printers kept in the upper of two type cases.

clue.text: Odd airline's dance

parts.note: rum is British slang for strange
BA is British Airways

explanation.surface: A strange carrier has its own peculiar dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum is old-fashioned British slang for peculiar, as in 'a rum business'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance with swaying hip movements, one example of a dance.

clue.text: What Musashi Miyamoto eats?

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two names

explanation.surface: A question about the diet of Japan's most famous swordsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Miyamoto Musashi was a legendary 17th-century Japanese swordsman; 'eats' is a sly signal, since his name literally takes in the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Sashimi is thinly sliced raw fish, a classic Japanese dish a Japanese warrior might well eat.

clue.text: Suffer in German and therefore in Latin

parts.note: und is German for and
ergo is Latin for therefore

explanation.surface: Someone endures hardship in two languages at once.
explanation.walkthrough: Each 'in' names a language to translate into, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo an ordeal is to experience or endure it, which is what suffering an ordeal means.

clue.text: Reeves' assistant, say, screwed up idea

indicators.note: something screwed up is crumpled or botched, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A political helper to the Chancellor has botched a policy idea.
explanation.walkthrough: Rachel Reeves became Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer in 2024; 'say' marks her assistant as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A politician's assistant is called an aide, a helper or adviser to a senior official.

clue.text: Cheats with every second bullet boring outraged readers

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into, so one group goes inside another
something outraged is thrown into turmoil, so these letters are put in disorder

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: taking every second item means keeping alternate ones, starting from the second

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Fraudsters and a stray bullet trouble readers who are furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheats' looks like a verb, but it is a plural noun for people who are unfaithful to a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is unfaithful to a spouse is said to cheat on them, so people committing adultery are cheats.

clue.text: Source of pressure for Putin running amok includes wild romp before start of talks

indicators.note: to include is to hold within, so one group sits inside the other
running can mean moving or in motion, so these letters move about

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something wild is unruly, so these letters are let loose into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Putin, out of control, uses an orgy recorded before negotiations as leverage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putin' belongs to the definition, not the anagram fodder; 'running amok' looks like one phrase but splits into indicator and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Kompromat is Russian for compromising material, damaging information gathered to blackmail or coerce someone, a tool of Russian intelligence.

clue.text: Publish in haste, lacking wherewithal to make papyrus

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put a book or statement out hurriedly
second meaning, read as two words: out of the reed-like plant papyrus is made from

explanation.surface: An Egyptian scribe rushes a text into print before the papyrus runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is whimsical: papyrus comes from a sedge, a rush-like plant, so to be 'out' of it is to lack the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: To rush something out is to release it hurriedly, and 'out' of rush means having none of the plant used for papyrus.

clue.text: Commonwealth partner opposed to fruit being cut short twice

indicators.note: cutting a word short trims its end, and doing it twice removes two final letters

parts.note: anti means against
a guava is a tropical fruit

explanation.surface: A fellow member nation objects to fruit being rationed again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Two cuts remove the final VA from the tropical fruit, leaving GUA.
explanation.definitionFit: Antigua, with Barbuda, is a Caribbean nation that belongs to the Commonwealth, the association of former British territories.

clue.text: Kremlin-style (dis)information might keep a wrong 'un up?

parts.note: taken as written
a git is a British insult for a contemptible person
with the clue's final 'up', to keep up is to prop, here placed below the person it supports

explanation.surface: Kremlin spin might be used to keep a rogue regime afloat.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrasal verb 'keep … up' wraps round its object, and in a down entry the support naturally sits underneath. Git is mild British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitprop is Soviet-originated political propaganda, from the Kremlin's department of agitation and propaganda, spreading slanted or false messages.

clue.text: Such transparency is not made with glass

indicators.note: to be made is to be constructed, so the letters are built into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A riddle: this kind of see-through quality does not come from a windowpane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transparency' suggests clear glass, but it means political openness. The 'Such' points back to the Soviet theme of the neighbouring clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasnost was Gorbachev's 1980s Soviet policy of openness in government, allowing more public information and debate.

clue.text: Modest fare returned to pub — followed by a spasm

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: the fare on offer is listed on the menu
PH is the map abbreviation for public house
taken as written
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: Plain food sent back to the bar, and then the diner has a seizure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modest fare' reads as one phrase about simple food, but 'Modest' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone modest in manner speaks without forcefulness or insistence, which is to say without emphasis.

clue.text: Require leads to end now; the act is looming

indicators.note: the leads of words are their front letters, so the opening letter of each is kept

parts.words: end now; the act is looming
parts.note: the opening letters of the six words

explanation.surface: A demand to wrap things up now, because the deed is imminent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' looks like 'results in', a near synonym of the answer, but it signals first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: If one thing entails another, it necessarily involves or calls for it, so entail is a synonym of need.

clue.text: Still a road to — or from — the Big Apple

parts.note: taken as written
the Big Apple is a nickname for New York
a way is a route, leading either to a place or from it

explanation.surface: There is still a road heading into or out of New York City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adjective meaning motionless, but it is the adverb meaning nevertheless.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean nevertheless or regardless, used when continuing despite something just said.

clue.text: Nothing emptied restaurant like an old club chairman in a blazer?

definitions.text: old club chairman in a blazer?
definitions.note: the definition borrows 'old' to complete the phrase 'old fart'

indicators.note: a thing emptied has had its contents removed, so the inner letters go and only the ends remain

parts.note: FA is short for 'sweet Fanny Adams', British slang for nothing at all
only the outer letters are left

explanation.surface: A stuffy club chairman in a blazer clears the dining room of everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet FA, short for 'sweet Fanny Adams', is British slang for nothing. The surface also hints at the literal smell that empties a room.
explanation.definitionFit: An 'old fart' is a fusty, conservative old person, a fair caricature of a blazered elderly club official.

clue.text: 'I could be a toolmaker' — Starmer's first lie on the radio

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

indicators.note: on the radio we hear words rather than see them, so the sound is what counts

parts.note: a myth is a falsehood

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer, the son of a toolmaker, tells a fib on a radio interview.
explanation.walkthrough: Starmer, Britain's Labour Prime Minister, often mentions his father was a toolmaker. The definition is spoken by the answer itself: a smith might make tools.
explanation.definitionFit: A smith works metal, and blacksmiths traditionally forged hand tools, so a smith may well be a maker of tools.

clue.text: Poetry in motion has new disorder

indicators.note: things in motion are shifting position, so these letters move into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: The graceful phrase 'poetry in motion' has acquired a fresh untidiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poetry in motion' is a stock phrase for graceful movement, but here it splits into fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics entropy measures the randomness of a system, and in general use it means a decline into chaos.

clue.text: Pepper setter, protected by horse

indicators.note: what is protected is surrounded by its guard, so one group sits inside another

parts.note: a pinto is a piebald horse
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: The setter, shielded by a horse, is being peppered with something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' could be a dog, but in crosswords it is the compiler, who becomes ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimento is a sweet red pepper, the kind stuffed into green olives, so it is one kind of pepper.

clue.text: Such as Shere Khan heard here?

indicators.note: what is heard reaches us as sound, so a word that sounds the same is wanted

parts.note: Shere Khan is the tiger in Kipling's The Jungle Book

explanation.surface: A question asking where the Jungle Book's tiger might be heard prowling.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British accent without the final R, tiger and the Russian forest word sound the same. 'here' is the definition: the place where such a big cat lives.
explanation.definitionFit: The taiga is the vast northern coniferous forest of Siberia, the home of the Siberian tiger.

clue.text: Paid off bill, including cut for joint

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it inside, so one group goes within another

parts.note: a bill is a poster or advertisement, AD for short
a mortise is a slot cut in wood to take a tenon

explanation.surface: Someone settled the account, including a discount on a cut of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut for joint' suggests butchery, but it is woodwork: the mortise-and-tenon joint.
explanation.definitionFit: To amortise a debt is to settle it gradually through regular instalments until it is cleared.
